title: The Bike That Wouldn't Wait
author: Oakman Academy
body:
Ravi found the bike behind Mr Okafor's shed, leaning against a stack of plant pots like it had given up. The frame was the colour of a conker, the seat was cracked, and the back brake was missing entirely, just a stub of cable poking out where it should have been. Mr Okafor said Ravi could have it if he could fix it himself.

"By Saturday?" Ravi asked. "There's a race on Saturday. Down Hollow Lane, past the allotments, first to the old oak wins."

"Saturday's four days away," said Mr Okafor, wiping his hands on a rag. "Plenty of time, if you don't waste it talking to me."

Ravi spent that evening at the kitchen table with the wheel between his knees, oil turning his fingers the colour of the frame. His dad found a brake part in a drawer of old bicycle bits, but it was the wrong size, too small for the fork by half a centimetre. The bike shop in town didn't have the right one either. It would have to be ordered, and it wouldn't come until Monday.

"You could just not race," said his sister Priya, who had a bike with gears and a bell and, most importantly, two working brakes.

Ravi didn't say anything, but he kept working. He found that if he pedalled backwards hard, the chain caught and slowed the back wheel enough to stop, clumsily, in a lurch rather than a smooth glide. He practised it up and down the lane until his legs ached and the streetlights came on, wobbling to a stop again and again by the postbox.

On Saturday morning six children lined up at the top of Hollow Lane. Ravi's chain rattled and his tyres were a little flat, but he had his backwards-pedal trick ready, and Mr Okafor stood at the finish line with his arms crossed, watching.

The race began, and Priya shot ahead on her gleaming bike, laughing over her shoulder. Ravi pedalled hard, elbows out, keeping the conker-coloured bike as steady as he could over the bumps. He was gaining, slowly, when he heard a hiss and a wobble ahead of him — Priya's front tyre had caught a thorn from the hedge and was sagging flat.

She wasn't hurt, just annoyed, hopping off and inspecting the tyre with her hands on her hips. Ravi rolled up beside her, pedalled backwards to lurch to a stop, and held out a hand.

"Race is over anyway," he said. "Walk back with me?"

They pushed both bikes home together, Ravi's chain still rattling, Priya grumbling cheerfully about thorns, and neither of them mentioned who would have won.
prompts: What was wrong with the bike Ravi found behind Mr Okafor's shed?
Why do you think Ravi kept practising his 'backwards-pedal trick' even though his legs ached?
If your bike broke right before a big race, what would you do?

vocabulary.meaning: to move suddenly and unsteadily
shining brightly
shaking unsteadily from side to side
sinking or bulging downward from pressure or weakness

title: The Octopus With Nine Brains
author: Oakman Academy
body:
If you shook hands with an octopus, you would be shaking hands with something that thinks with its arms as much as its head. An octopus has one brain in the middle of its body, but each of its eight arms also has its own cluster of nerves, almost like a small brain of its own. Scientists think this is why an octopus can explore a rock pool with one arm while another arm is doing something completely different, such as prising open a shell for dinner. More than half of an octopus's nerve cells are out in its arms rather than in its central brain.

That is strange enough, but an octopus is full of surprises. It has not one heart but three. Two small hearts pump blood to the gills, and a third, larger heart pumps blood around the rest of the body. When an octopus swims hard, the large heart actually stops beating for a moment, which is one reason octopuses prefer to crawl along the seabed rather than swim if they can help it — swimming tires them out fast.

The blood itself is blue, not red. Human blood is red because it carries oxygen using a substance called haemoglobin, which contains iron. Octopus blood uses a different substance called haemocyanin, which contains copper instead, and copper turns the blood pale blue. This blue blood is especially good at carrying oxygen in cold water, which helps octopuses that live in the chilly depths of the ocean.

Perhaps the most famous octopus trick is changing colour. Skin cells called chromatophores can expand or shrink in less than a second, letting an octopus flush red with alarm, fade to sandy grey to hide against the seabed, or even ripple with stripes to startle a hungry fish. Some octopuses can also change the texture of their skin, puckering it into bumps and ridges so that smooth flesh suddenly looks exactly like knobbly coral. Curiously, most scientists believe octopuses cannot actually see colour themselves — yet they still manage to match the colours around them almost perfectly, and nobody is entirely sure how.

Octopuses are also famous for escaping. Because they have no bones at all, an octopus can squeeze its whole body through any gap wider than its beak, which is the only hard part it has. Aquarium keepers have found octopuses squeezing out of sealed tanks at night, crossing the floor, and slipping into a neighbouring tank to eat the fish, before returning to their own tank before morning as if nothing had happened.

An animal with three hearts, blue blood, nine centres of thought, and the ability to vanish through a gap the size of a coin — the octopus is one of the strangest and cleverest creatures in the sea.
prompts: How many hearts does an octopus have, and what does each one do?
Why do you think an octopus's arms have their own nerve clusters instead of everything being controlled by one brain?
Which fact about the octopus did you find the most surprising, and why?

vocabulary.meaning: skin cells that can change colour
the blue substance in octopus blood that carries oxygen
how a surface feels, for example smooth or bumpy
a building or tank where sea creatures are kept for people to see

title: The Bus Stop in November
author: Oakman Academy
body:
The morning comes in grey and slow,
my breath goes up like ghostly smoke.
The puddle by the postbox froze
and cracked beneath my wellies' poke.

Dad's coffee steams. He checks his phone.
The dog next door barks twice, then stops.
A magpie lands, then flies alone,
and lands again three gardens up.

I count the cars that splash on by,
the ones with wipers, ones without.
A red one, then a taxi, why
do drivers never look about?

My scarf has come undone again.
The bus is late — it's always late.
Dad says that we'll be fine, and then
the yellow lights blink round the gate.

We climb aboard, stamp off the cold,
find seats before the doors can shut.
The window fogs. My hand, so bold,
draws one small sun in all that mud.

By half past eight the sky turns pale,
a thin white line above the hill.
November mornings never fail
to make me shiver, make me still —

and yet I like this small parade:
the magpie, puddle, steaming cup,
the sun I drew and slowly fade,
the bus that always, always turns up.
prompts: What things does the child notice while waiting at the bus stop?
How can you tell the child doesn't really mind the cold November mornings, even though they shiver?
What small everyday things make you feel happy, like the child's drawing on the foggy window?

vocabulary.meaning: like a ghost; pale, misty or strange
a black-and-white bird known for its loud chattering call
a line of people or things passing by, or a display of something
rubber boots worn to keep feet dry, short for wellington boots

title: The Den at the End of the Garden
author: Oakman Academy
body:
Tom and Elsie built the den out of everything the garden could spare: three broken deckchairs, a length of old carpet, and a blue tarpaulin that used to cover the woodpile. It stood at the end of the garden behind the raspberry canes, and by the summer holidays it had a proper doorway, a "window" made from a picture frame with no glass in it, and a rule, written by Tom in marker pen on a paper plate: NO LITTLE SISTERS.

Elsie was eight and Tom was ten, and as far as Tom was concerned, two years was more than enough of a gap to matter. He had built the den with his friend Dev on a Tuesday when it rained, and he wanted somewhere that was only his — no sharing, no little sister trailing in with her plastic dinosaurs and wanting to play shops.

Elsie didn't argue. She simply built her own den three metres away, out of the washing line prop and an old bedsheet, and hung a sign on it that said NO BROTHERS, MEGA SECRET CLUB, KEEP OUT written in her best bubble writing with a smiley face at the end, which annoyed Tom more than he expected.

For a week the two dens stood facing each other across the grass like small, stubborn countries. Then, on a Thursday, a real storm came through — not a rainy afternoon but proper wind, the kind that rattled the fence panels and sent the trampoline net flapping. Tom's tarpaulin ripped clean off its string in the night. In the morning both dens were flattened, the paper plate rule soaked through and unreadable, Elsie's bedsheet wrapped round the rose bush like a strange white flag.

They stood surveying the wreckage together without really meaning to.

"We could build one," Elsie said carefully, "that's big enough for both dens' stuff. Yours and mine."

Tom looked at the tangled sheet, the soggy carpet, the picture-frame window lying face-down in the mud, and decided that building one big den sounded like considerably less work than building two small ones twice.

They spent the whole of Saturday on it, using both tarpaulins tied together with the washing line prop as the main pole. Elsie's dinosaurs got a shelf made from a broken plant pot tray. Tom's comics got a dry corner under the thickest bit of tarpaulin. The new sign, which they wrote together, simply said DEN — and underneath, in smaller writing, ASK FIRST, which felt, to both of them, exactly fair.
prompts: What happened to both dens during the storm?
Why do you think Tom's rule annoyed him so much when Elsie copied it for her own den?
Would you rather have your own den or share one with a brother or sister? Why?

vocabulary.meaning: looking carefully at something to understand it
twisted together in a messy way
by a large amount
refusing to change or give in

title: Mia and the Deep End
author: Oakman Academy
body:
Mia had a rule about the deep end: she didn't go in it. Not with armbands, not holding the side, not even to touch the rope with one finger and swim straight back. The deep end was where the water turned from pale blue to dark blue, where her feet couldn't find the bottom, and where, as far as Mia was concerned, that was that.

"It's exactly the same water," said her swimming teacher, Mr Adeyemi, for what felt like the hundredth time. "Just more of it underneath you."

"That's the problem," said Mia. "More of it underneath me."

Every Tuesday she swam neat, careful lengths in the shallow end while the rest of her class practised dives off the side in the deep end, laughing and splashing and generally having, Mia thought, an unfairly good time. She told herself she didn't mind. Mostly, she didn't.

Then came the trip to Wren Lake with her cousin Dara, who was seven and fearless and already wading in up to her knees before anyone had put the picnic down. Mia stood at the edge with her toes in the mud, watching Dara splash further out, laughing, calling back over her shoulder — and then not laughing. Dara had gone quiet and was paddling in one spot, arms working hard, not really going anywhere, her chin dipping under and coming back up.

Mia didn't decide to go in. Her feet decided for her, and then the water was at her waist, her chest, and she was swimming — properly swimming, the strokes Mr Adeyemi had drilled into her a hundred times in the shallow end — until she reached Dara and got an arm under her and turned them both back towards the shore, kicking hard, not once looking down at how much water was underneath them.

Dara, it turned out, had only been tired, not truly in danger, and was more embarrassed than frightened once they reached the shallows. But Mia stood there afterwards, water streaming off her, heart going like a drum, and realised something odd: she had just swum in water she couldn't touch the bottom of, and the sky hadn't fallen in.

The next Tuesday, she walked to the deep end before Mr Adeyemi could even ask, put one hand on the rope, and then, before she could think better of it, let go.

"Well," said Mr Adeyemi, trying not to grin too widely. "That's more of it underneath you, and here you still are."

"Here I still am," said Mia, and swam a slow, wobbly length, grinning the whole way across.
prompts: Why did Mia have a rule about never going in the deep end?
How can you tell that Mia didn't stop to think before she swam out to help Dara?
Have you ever done something brave without really deciding to? What happened?
essayPrompt: Explain how Mia changes from the beginning of the story to the end. Use two things she says or does to support your answer.

not afraid of anything

title: Emperor Penguins: The Coldest Nursery on Earth
author: Oakman Academy
body:
In the middle of the Antarctic winter, when the sun does not rise for weeks and temperatures fall to minus sixty degrees, a male emperor penguin stands completely still for over two months, balancing a single egg on his feet.

Emperor penguins are the only animals that breed during the Antarctic winter, when almost everything else has fled north to warmer water. In April, after the female lays one egg, she carefully passes it to her mate, who tucks it onto the tops of his feet and covers it with a warm fold of skin and feathers called a brood pouch. From that moment, the father does not move far, does not eat, and does not let the egg touch the ice, not even for a second, or the cold would kill the chick inside within minutes.

While the father waits, the mother makes an extraordinary journey. She walks, sometimes for days, across the frozen sea to reach open water, where she can finally eat after weeks of fasting, feasting on fish and small shrimp-like creatures called krill to build her strength back up.

Back on the ice, thousands of fathers huddle together in a tight, shuffling crowd to survive the cold. Scientists have studied these huddles closely and found something remarkable: the penguins take turns. The birds on the outside, facing the full force of the wind, slowly shuffle around the edge of the group over time until they end up sheltered in the warm middle, while the ones who have been warm move outward to take their turn facing the wind. In this way, no single penguin freezes while the others stay comfortable — the whole group survives together, turn by turn.

By the time the egg hatches, in July or August, the father may have gone without food for over three months and lost nearly half his body weight. If the mother has not yet returned, he can feed the newly hatched chick a special milky substance made in his own throat, just enough to keep it alive for a few more days.

When the mother finally returns, fat and full from the ocean, she recognises her mate and chick by their calls alone, among thousands of identical-looking penguins, and takes over feeding while the exhausted father finally makes his own long walk to the sea to eat for the first time in months.

Few animals endure a winter like the emperor penguin's, standing through the coldest, darkest season on Earth for the sake of a single egg.
prompts: How does a father emperor penguin keep the egg safe and warm?
Why do you think the penguins take turns being on the outside and inside of the huddle?
Which part of the emperor penguin's winter would be hardest for you to do? Why?

vocabulary.meaning: a warm fold of skin and feathers a penguin uses to cover its egg
tiny shrimp-like creatures that many sea animals eat
a close, tightly packed group, often for warmth
going without food for a period of time

title: The Attic Astronaut
author: Oakman Academy
body:
Up the ladder, through the hatch,
past the boxes, past the tank
where Dad keeps spare bits of thatch,
there's a place that no one's ranked

on any map of anywhere —
my attic base, my launch, my ship,
with a colander for a helmet's flare
and a torch beam for a trip

to the moon, or maybe Mars,
or a planet no one's named,
past a hundred paper stars
that I stuck up and half-framed.

Mission Control (that's Mum downstairs)
calls up "Tea's ready, spaceman, come!"
I radio back through cobweb air,
"Just orbiting — five minutes, Mum."

Down below the real world waits,
with real tea and real chairs,
but up here past the two loft gates
I'm the first to breathe this air.

Nobody else has been this far
in a dusty, cardboard, wooden place —
the bravest, strangest sort of star,
an astronaut of attic space.
prompts: What does the child use as a helmet in the attic?
How can you tell the attic feels like a completely different world to the child, even though it's part of their own house?
If you could turn any room or space at home into somewhere imaginary, what would you turn it into?

vocabulary.meaning: a small door or opening, often in a floor or ceiling
a bowl with holes in it, used for draining food like pasta
travelling in a circle around something, like a planet around the sun
a thin, sticky web spun by a spider

title: The Case of the Missing Tortoise
author: Oakman Academy
body:
Mrs Featherstone's tortoise, Napoleon, had been missing for two days, which should have been impossible, because Napoleon moved at roughly the speed of a Tuesday and had never in his eleven years made it past the garden gate.

"He can't have gone far," said Jayden, standing at the fence with his best friend Aliyah, both of them staring at the empty patch of lettuce where Napoleon usually sat. "He's a tortoise. He's basically a very slow rock."

"Rocks don't go missing," said Aliyah, crouching down to look under the hedge. "Something must have happened to him."

They searched the obvious places first — behind the shed, under the wheelbarrow, inside the greenhouse where it was warm — but Napoleon was nowhere. Then Aliyah noticed something: a trail of flattened grass leading away from the lettuce patch, curving round the compost heap and disappearing under the fence into the next garden along, which belonged to old Mr Grewal, who nobody in the street had spoken to properly since he'd moved in.

"We can't just go into his garden," said Jayden.

"We're not going in," said Aliyah. "We're going to knock on his door like normal people and ask a normal question."

Mr Grewal answered on the third knock, looking faintly surprised that anyone had knocked at all. When Aliyah explained about the missing tortoise, his face changed completely — from surprised to something closer to caught out.

"Ah," he said. "You'd better come round the back."

In Mr Grewal's garden, behind a row of runner beans, was a tortoise-sized wooden ramp leading into a little enclosure lined with straw — and there, munching contentedly on a dandelion, was Napoleon, looking not remotely sorry for himself.

"He kept getting under my fence to eat my strawberries," Mr Grewal explained. "So I built a proper little run for him here, thinking he'd stay a day and wander home. He didn't want to leave. I was going to knock on Mrs Featherstone's door this evening, honestly — I didn't want her to worry any longer than that."

Aliyah and Jayden carried Napoleon home between them in a laundry basket, past the compost heap, back to the lettuce patch, where Mrs Featherstone cried with relief and then laughed when she heard about the strawberries. As for Mr Grewal, he came round himself that evening with a bag of extra strawberry plants "for the tortoise, so he's got his own," and stayed for tea, which was the first time, Jayden's mum said later, that anyone on the street had managed to get him through a front door.
prompts: Where did Jayden and Aliyah eventually find Napoleon the tortoise?
Why do you think Mr Grewal looked 'caught out' when Aliyah asked about the missing tortoise?
Do you think Mr Grewal should have told Mrs Featherstone sooner? What would you have done?

vocabulary.meaning: pressed down flat
a fenced or walled area used to keep an animal in
in a happy, satisfied way
even slightly (used to mean 'at all')

title: Grandad's Jar of Buttons
author: Oakman Academy
body:
On the windowsill of Grandad's workshop sat a jar of buttons, hundreds of them, every colour and size, collected over sixty years from coats and shirts that had long since worn out and been thrown away. Freya had been fascinated by that jar since she was small enough to need both hands to lift it.

"Every single one has a story," Grandad always said, "if you know where to look for it."

That summer, Freya was staying with Grandad for two weeks while her parents sorted out the new house, and she had decided, privately, that she would rather be doing almost anything else. There was no internet in the workshop, no friends nearby, and Grandad moved and talked so slowly that Freya had to force herself not to finish his sentences.

On the third rainy afternoon, bored enough to try anything, she asked about the buttons. Grandad's face lifted in a way she hadn't seen since she'd arrived.

He picked out a flat brass one first. "Off my father's work coat. He wore it down the mine every day for thirty years — see how smooth it's gone, from his hand doing it up in the dark before dawn." Then a small pearly one. "Your grandmother's wedding dress. Lost one button walking down the aisle, and I found it in my pocket weeks later, still had the thread attached."

One by one, Freya turned the buttons over in her fingers as Grandad told her about a coat he'd worn to his first job interview, a cardigan her own mother had loved as a baby, a duffel coat button chewed slightly by a dog neither of them had ever met but who apparently used to steal socks off the washing line.

By the end of the afternoon, Freya had heard more about her family in two hours than she had in her whole life put together, and the rain outside the window had stopped without either of them noticing.

The next day, Grandad handed her a small tin. "Every button needs a keeper," he said, "once it's told its story. Yours now." Inside were a dozen buttons he'd already picked out, ready for her to learn properly — not for looking pretty on a windowsill, but for handing on.

Freya kept the tin on her own windowsill after that, and whenever anyone asked why she had a box of old buttons, she found she couldn't explain it quickly at all, only that each one, if you knew where to look, had rather a good story attached.
prompts: What did Grandad tell Freya was special about the flat brass button?
Why do you think Freya's feelings about staying with Grandad changed after that rainy afternoon?
If you had a jar of objects that told stories about your family, what would be in it?

vocabulary.meaning: extremely interested in something
keeping a thought or feeling to yourself, not saying it aloud
a walkway between rows, such as in a church during a wedding
a thick coat with a hood, fastened with toggles

title: The Lighthouse Keeper's Apprentice
author: Oakman Academy
body:
Sam had never liked storms, not even the small ones that just rattled the windows at home, so spending half-term with his grandmother at the lighthouse felt, to him, like a very unfair holiday.

"You get used to it," said his grandmother, Nan Okonkwo, who had kept the light for eleven years, ever since the lighthouse had been handed over from the old official keepers to a small team of local volunteers. "The sea doesn't stop being loud just because you're scared of it. Might as well learn its noises."

On his first night, a proper gale blew in, rain slamming sideways against the glass, the whole tower seeming to hum under his feet. Sam lay in the narrow bed at the top of the tower with his eyes wide open, listening to his grandmother's slow footsteps climbing the spiral stairs to check the light, over and over, all through the night.

By the third day the wind had calmed enough that Nan Okonkwo let him climb the stairs with her for the evening check. The lamp room at the very top was smaller than Sam expected, a great glass lens turning slowly in the middle, throwing a long beam out across water the colour of pewter.

"Ships out there," she said, "trust that this beam is exactly where it should be, exactly when it should be, every single night. Fishermen, ferries, even big cargo ships passing at midnight — they steer by it without ever seeing us at all."

That night the wind picked up again, harder than before, and partway through Sam heard his grandmother's radio crackle — a small fishing boat, caught out later than planned, radioing in that they could see the light but were struggling against the current near the rocks. Nan Okonkwo stayed calm, talking steadily into the radio, giving directions, checking the lamp was turning properly, moving without any wasted motion at all.

Sam, without really deciding to, found himself holding the torch steady for her at the workbench, fetching the logbook when she asked, staying quiet exactly when quiet was needed. It was well past midnight before the fishing boat radioed back that they'd found safe water, voices tinny and relieved through the crackle.

Only afterwards, back in the narrow bed, did Sam notice that he'd sat through the whole storm without once putting his hands over his ears.

"Not bad," said his grandmother from the doorway, "for someone who doesn't like storms."

"I still don't," said Sam. "But I like knowing what the light's for now. That helps."

Nan Okonkwo smiled and turned off the lamp on the landing, leaving the real light, high above them, still turning steadily through the dark.
prompts: What job did Sam do to help his grandmother during the emergency with the fishing boat?
How can you tell that Sam has changed by the end of the story, even though he says he 'still doesn't' like storms?
Has learning how something works ever made you feel less scared of it? Tell me about it.
essayPrompt: Explain how Sam changes during his stay at the lighthouse. Use two things he does or says to support your answer.

vocabulary.meaning: a very strong wind
in a calm, controlled and continuous way
sounding thin and metallic, like through a small speaker
a book used to record events, kept by ships or lighthouses
